title: The Hokule'a Sails to Tahiti
text:
By the 1970s many scholars believed that the Polynesian settlement of the Pacific had happened largely by accident, with canoes drifting to new islands. Hawaiians had lost the knowledge of how their ancestors navigated. In 1973 the anthropologist Ben Finney, the artist Herb Kane and the sailor Tommy Holmes founded the Polynesian Voyaging Society to test the question by sailing a traditional canoe to Tahiti without instruments.

They built Hokule'a, a double-hulled voyaging canoe about 19 meters long. But no Hawaiian could navigate it in the old way. They found Mau Piailug, a master navigator from the tiny island of Satawal in Micronesia, one of the last people trained in traditional wayfinding, who read the stars, the swells, the wind and the birds.

The canoe left Maui on 1 May 1976. The voyage was hard on the crew in more ways than one. Tensions grew between some of the Hawaiian crew members and the scientists, and there were quarrels and fights on board. Through it all Mau kept his course, guiding the canoe by stars and ocean swells across more than 4,000 kilometers of open sea.

On 4 June Hokule'a reached Papeete, where a huge crowd, reported at around 17,000 people, came out to greet it. Mau, upset by the conflict on board, flew home rather than sail back. He later returned to teach Hawaiian Nainoa Thompson, who revived the art for a new generation.
lesson: Reviving lost knowledge takes respect for the people who still hold it. A team's purpose can survive conflict, but healing it afterward matters for the next voyage.
people: Mau Piailug, Ben Finney, Herb Kane, Tommy Holmes, Nainoa Thompson
location: Pacific Ocean, from Maui, Hawaii, USA, to Papeete, Tahiti (French Polynesia)
source: Ben Finney, Hokule'a: The Way to Tahiti (1979)
